_comment: The item bank for the Archaea And Extreme Places game (Sorter: bacterium / archaean / neither). Every classification was fact-checked (see the unit notes). Rounds: 1 = the lesson, 2 = the traps, 3 = far past the lesson (meant to be almost impossible at the end). 'core' items are in every draw. 'trap' names the mistake a student most likely made when the item is wrong.

bin_hints.bacterium: a prokaryote in the domain Bacteria
bin_hints.archaean: a prokaryote in the domain Archaea
bin_hints.neither: it has a nucleus, or it is not a cell

rules: No nucleus and a cell: it is a bacterium or an archaean.
A nucleus, or not a cell at all (a virus): neither.
A methanogen (a microbe that lives by making methane) is always an archaean.
Where it lives does not decide it: bacteria live in hot, salty and deep places too.

pool.text: A cyanobacterium in a pond
pool.why: It has no nucleus and is in the domain Bacteria. Cyanobacteria make food using light.

pool.text: A bacterium that turns milk into yoghurt
pool.why: It has no nucleus and is in the domain Bacteria.

pool.text: A rod-shaped bacillus from the soil
pool.why: A bacillus is a rod-shaped bacterium.

pool.text: A decomposer in a compost heap that breaks down dead leaves
pool.why: Decomposer bacteria feed on dead material. It has no nucleus.

pool.text: A coccus on your skin
pool.why: A coccus is a spherical bacterium.

pool.text: A methane-making microbe in a cow's stomach
pool.why: Every methanogen (methane-making microbe) is an archaean. It needs no oxygen.

pool.text: A methane-making microbe in swamp mud
pool.why: Every methanogen (methane-making microbe) is an archaean. It needs no oxygen.

pool.text: A methane-making microbe in a sewage works
pool.why: Methanogens are archaea, and sewage has no oxygen for them to avoid.

pool.text: A methane-making microbe in a rice paddy
pool.why: Waterlogged mud has no oxygen: methanogens, which are archaea, live there.

pool.text: A microbe that can grow at 113 °C beside a deep-sea vent
pool.why: Only archaea are known to grow above about 100 °C. It has no nucleus, and it is not a bacterium.

pool.text: A human cheek cell
pool.why: It has a nucleus, so it is a eukaryote.

pool.text: A yeast cell
pool.why: Yeast is a single-celled fungus. It has a nucleus.

pool.text: A flu virus
pool.why: A virus is not a cell, so it is not a bacterium or an archaean.

pool.text: An amoeba
pool.why: An amoeba is a single cell, but it has a nucleus.

pool.text: A cell from a green leaf
pool.why: A plant cell has a nucleus.

rounds.name: Round 2: where it lives is a trap

pool.text: A heat-loving microbe from a hot spring in Yellowstone, the source of the enzyme used in PCR tests
pool.why: It loves heat, but it is a bacterium. A hot place does not make a microbe an archaean.

pool.text: A cyanobacterium forming orange mats at the edge of a hot spring
pool.why: Cyanobacteria are bacteria, and some live in hot springs.

pool.text: A microbe that survives huge doses of radiation and was found in tinned meat
pool.why: It is extreme, but it is a bacterium. Extreme does not mean archaean.

pool.text: The sulfur-using bacteria that live inside giant tube worms at a deep-sea vent
pool.why: Vents have archaea, but these are chemosynthetic bacteria.

pool.text: A 'blue-green alga' that blooms on a lake in summer
pool.why: 'Blue-green algae' are cyanobacteria. They have no nucleus, so they are bacteria.

pool.text: Halobacterium, a salt-loving microbe from a very salty lake
pool.why: Its name says 'bacterium', but it is an archaean. It was named before archaea were recognised.

pool.text: A methane-making microbe in the human gut
pool.why: It lives in a body, as many bacteria do, but all methane-makers are archaea.

pool.text: A microbe that grows at 122 °C under very high pressure in the lab
pool.why: The record for the hottest growth is held by an archaean.

pool.text: A single-celled red alga that lives in a hot, acidic spring
pool.why: It has a nucleus, so it is a eukaryote, even in a hot spring.

pool.text: A yeast that grows in the very salty brine of soy sauce
pool.why: Yeast is a fungus with a nucleus. Salt does not make it an archaean.

pool.text: A virus that infects bacteria
pool.why: A virus is not a cell, so it is neither.

pool.text: A virus that infects archaea
pool.why: A virus is not a cell, even if its host is an archaean.

pool.text: A single-celled alga that turns a very salty lake pink
pool.why: It is an alga with a nucleus. Some pink lakes also hold bacteria and archaea, but this cell has a nucleus.

pool.text: A cell with no nucleus whose cell wall is made of peptidoglycan
pool.why: Peptidoglycan is found only in bacterial cell walls. Archaea have a different cell wall chemistry.

pool.text: A cell with no nucleus that makes its own food from light and gives out oxygen
pool.why: Only cyanobacteria among the prokaryotes make oxygen by photosynthesis. It is a bacterium.

pool.text: The cells that turn a pond green and slimy in summer, each with no nucleus
pool.why: Pond blooms like this are often cyanobacteria. With no nucleus, they are bacteria.

pool.text: A cell with no nucleus living in the cells of a giant tube worm
pool.why: They are chemosynthetic bacteria. They are inside an animal, but they are not an archaean.

pool.text: A cell with no nucleus that lives by making methane
pool.why: Cells that live by making methane (methanogens) are all archaea.

pool.text: A cell with no nucleus, from a spring, that grows at 108 °C
pool.why: Only archaea are known to grow above about 100 °C.

pool.text: A methane-making microbe in a termite's gut
pool.why: Methanogens are archaea, in a termite as in a cow.

pool.text: A single-celled protist in a termite's gut that helps to digest wood
pool.why: It has a nucleus. The termite's gut holds bacteria, archaea and protists.

pool.text: A mitochondrion inside one of your cells, which has its own circle of DNA and divides
pool.why: It is part of a cell, not a cell. It looks a little like a bacterium, but it is neither.

pool.text: A bacteriophage, a virus with a tail that injects its DNA into a bacterium
pool.why: A virus is not a cell, so it is neither.

pool.text: A single-celled fungus living in the gut of a beetle
pool.why: A fungus has a nucleus, so it is a eukaryote.

pool.text: A cell from a mould growing on stale bread
pool.why: A fungal cell has a nucleus.

pool.text: A cell with no nucleus whose membrane fats are joined by ether bonds
pool.why: Ether-linked membrane lipids are a mark of archaea. Bacteria have ester links.

pool.text: A cell with a nucleus and a cell wall that makes its own food from light
pool.why: A plant or algal cell has a nucleus and a cell wall. A cell wall does not make it a prokaryote.

mistakes.bacterium>archaean: Where it lives does not decide it. Bacteria live in hot, salty and deep places too.
mistakes.archaean>bacterium: Archaea have no nucleus either, and they look like bacteria, so this is an easy mistake. They are a separate domain.
mistakes.neither>bacterium: Check for a nucleus first. This one has a nucleus, or it is not a cell at all.
mistakes.neither>archaean: Check for a nucleus first. This one has a nucleus, or it is not a cell at all.
mistakes.bacterium>neither: A cell with no nucleus is a prokaryote. A prokaryote is a bacterium or an archaean.
mistakes.archaean>neither: A cell with no nucleus is a prokaryote. A prokaryote is a bacterium or an archaean.
